806.title: Dharma at the lake
806.hook: one brother may live: Yudhishthira chooses Nakula, and the yaksha shows who he really is

segments.voice: The questions are over, and the yaksha is satisfied. One of your brothers may live, he says. Choose. On the shore lie four of them. Bhima, whose strength the family leans on. Arjuna, the archer they'll need in any war to come. And the twins, Nakula and Sahadeva. Yudhishthira looks at them all, one by one, for a long moment. Then he names one, and the yaksha asks him why.
screen: `ONE BROTHER MAY LIVE.` → `FOUR ON THE SHORE.` → `CHOOSE.`

segments.voice: Let Nakula live, Yudhishthira says. Why him? Why not Bhima, so strong, or Arjuna, whom you all depend on? Yudhishthira answers: my father had two wives, Kunti and Madri. I am Kunti's son, and I'm alive. Let Madri have a living son too. He passes over the brothers who could win him a war, and chooses the one who keeps the family fair. The yaksha is delighted. Because you hold not being cruel higher than gain or pleasure, he says, let all four of your brothers live. And they stand up, as if from sleep. Then the stranger shows his face. He is Dharma himself, Yudhishthira's own father, and the deer that ran off with the fire-sticks was Dharma too. Here's the teaching, and it's one of the epic's biggest. The Sanskrit word is anrishamsya: not being cruel, keeping your heart open to the person a cold calculation would leave out. The Mahabharata ranks it among the highest dharma, and this is the moment that shows why Yudhishthira is called Dharmaraja, the king of dharma. Dharma here isn't a rulebook. It's the moment the clever move and the kind move split, and you take the kind one. Dharma grants him gifts: the fire-sticks back, a year in hiding where no one will know them, and a mind set on generosity, truth and self-discipline. Today the same choice comes small: who gets picked, who gets the bigger share, whose turn it is. Dharma's question isn't who helps me most. It's who would be left out.

807.title: five disguises, one promise
807.hook: the forest years are over, and to keep their word, five brothers and Draupadi must vanish for a year
807.carry: satya: keep your word, even when it humbles you
807.howItsDone: Retellings of the Virata book keep the disguise names (Kanka, Vallava, Brihannala, Sairandhri), and the year in hiding is told as a promise kept to the letter; Harishchandra and Rama are the stories Hindu families most often tell about keeping one's word.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dharma, the voice at the lake, revealed as Yudhishthira's own father, after a choice that put not being cruel above gain. Your line was dharma puts non-cruelty above gain.

segments.voice: One last year, lived among people, without being recognized. Those were the terms of the dice game, and if anyone sees through them, the exile begins again. So the five brothers and Draupadi sit together, and Yudhishthira asks each of them a question. Not where will you hide. What will you be? Where will you work, and as whom? They have chosen a kingdom to vanish into: the land of the Matsyas, ruled by King Virata. The Virata book opens with something close to a job interview, held in secret.
screen: `ONE YEAR, UNRECOGNIZED.` → `WHAT WILL YOU BE?` → `THE COURT OF KING VIRATA.`

segments.voice: Why go through with it at all? In the forest, Bhima begged Yudhishthira more than once to stop waiting and fight; the dice game was rigged. And Yudhishthira said no. I gave my word. That's the teaching under this whole year, and Hindus have a word for it: satya, truth, which includes the promise kept. In the stories Hindu families grow up on, King Harishchandra gives up his kingdom rather than break his word, and Rama goes to the forest so his father's promise stands. The Pandavas belong to that line. So listen to the answers. Yudhishthira will be Kanka, a Brahmin who plays dice with the king. The man whose love of dice cost them everything wears it as his cover. Bhima will be Vallava, the cook. Arjuna will hide his bowstring scars under bangles and live as Brihannala, who teaches dance to the palace women. Nakula will keep the horses, Sahadeva the cattle. And Draupadi, a queen, will serve a queen as Sairandhri, a maid who dresses hair. Their priest Dhaumya gives them rules for a king's house: don't take a seat that might be someone else's, speak when you're asked, don't show off. Princes become staff for a year, to keep a promise made to people who cheated them. Today, satya rarely costs a throne. It looks like the promise you made when it was easy, kept when it's embarrassing. In Hindu teaching, a word given is part of dharma.

808.title: weapons in the shami tree
808.hook: a bundle tied high in a shami tree near the cremation ground, and nobody wants to go near it
808.carry: why hindus honor the shami and their tools
808.howItsDone: In many regions the shami tree is worshipped at Dussehra (Vijayadashami), and popular tradition links the custom to the Pandavas' weapons; Ayudha Puja, the blessing of tools, is kept around the same days, especially in South India.

segments.voice: Yesterday: five disguises for Virata's court, built so the Pandavas could keep their word. Your line was satya: keep your word, even when it humbles you.
screen: `VIRATA: THE YEAR IN DISGUISE.` · `SATYA: THE PROMISE KEPT.`

segments.voice: A shami tree stands near a cremation ground outside King Virata's city. Thick branches, hard to climb, and a place people would rather walk past. Nakula climbs it. He ties a long bundle high in the branches, wrapped tight so the rain won't reach it. Inside is luggage that could end the whole disguise: Arjuna's bow, the Gandiva, and the brothers' other weapons. A wandering cook can't carry a bow every warrior knows on sight. So the weapons stay behind.
screen: `A SHAMI TREE BY THE CREMATION GROUND.` → `NAKULA CLIMBS.` → `THE WEAPONS STAY BEHIND.`

segments.voice: The text adds a grim, clever detail. To keep curious people away, the brothers tie a dead body in the tree too, and tell passing herdsmen it's an old family custom. Nobody climbs a tree like that. Then they enter the city one at a time: Yudhishthira with dice wrapped in cloth, Bhima with a ladle, Arjuna in women's ornaments. Draupadi walks the streets in one worn cloth until Queen Sudeshna calls her up, and when the queen worries the king will look at her, Draupadi says she has Gandharva husbands who guard her unseen. It's true, in its way: they're in the kitchen, the stables and at the dice table. And the bundle stays in the tree for a year. Here's why Hindus still care. The tree that kept the Pandavas' weapons is honored to this day. In many regions, at Dussehra, also called Vijayadashami, families worship the shami tree, and in some places people trade its leaves as gold. The popular telling links it to this story: the weapons coming back down at the year's end. Around the same days, many families keep Ayudha Puja. They clean and bless the tools of their work, books, a car, a laptop, a sewing machine, because in Hindu teaching work done rightly is an offering, and what serves it deserves respect. Today, look at what you work with. A tool set aside isn't forgotten. It's waiting, honored, for its day.

segments.voice: The disguises have held for months. Then the queen's brother comes to visit. His name is Kichaka. He commands King Virata's army, and the court is a little afraid of him. He sees the maid Sairandhri and wants her. She refuses him, plainly, and tells him she's protected. He doesn't care. He goes to his sister, the queen, and the queen sends Sairandhri to his house on an errand, to fetch wine. Draupadi knows exactly what this errand is.
screen: `THE QUEEN'S BROTHER, KICHAKA.` → `SHE REFUSES HIM.` → `AN ERRAND THAT IS A TRAP.`

segments.voice: At Kichaka's house he grabs at her. She breaks free and runs, straight into the royal court, where King Virata sits with Kanka at the dice. Kichaka chases her in, catches her by the hair, and kicks her to the floor in front of everyone. Bhima is there, and his face darkens; he stares at a big tree as if he means to tear it up for a club. Yudhishthira sees it, presses Bhima's toe, and says something like: looking for firewood, cook? Cut your trees somewhere else. But Draupadi doesn't stay quiet. From the floor she speaks to the king in his own court. What kind of king lets a woman be struck in front of him and does nothing? Then Kanka turns to her. Go to the queen's rooms. Your Gandharva husbands will act when the time is right. One word of recognition and the whole year is lost. Here is a teaching the Mahabharata returns to again and again: dharma is subtle. In the dice hall, when Draupadi asked her question, Bhishma told her the way of dharma is subtle and hard to see. Here two duties pull apart: the promise to stay hidden, and a husband's duty to protect. The epic doesn't pretend it's tidy, and it gives Draupadi the voice that names the wrong: a king's power exists to protect, the heart of raja dharma, the ruler's duty. Today, when duties collide, the epic won't let you call the cost nothing, and it won't let anyone silence the one who names the wrong.

segments.voice: It's night in King Virata's palace. Draupadi can't sleep. She gets up, crosses the dark courtyard, and goes to the kitchen, where the royal cook Vallava is asleep. She doesn't go to Yudhishthira. She goes to Bhima. She wakes him, and the first thing she says is a question: how can you sleep?

segments.voice: Then she tells him all of it, and the epic gives her room. Not only Kichaka. The whole road: the dice hall, the forest, a queen grinding sandal paste for another queen until her hands are rough, the king of the world playing dice for a living. She's grieving for all of them. And Bhima listens. The text says he holds her hands and weeps with her. Then the cook makes a plan. Tell Kichaka yes, he says. Meet him tonight in the dancing hall, empty after dark. I'll be waiting instead. Kichaka arrives dressed for a meeting and finds the cook. They fight, two strong men in an empty hall, and Bhima kills him. The court blames the hidden Gandharvas. When Kichaka's kinsmen turn on Sairandhri, Bhima rescues her again, and still nobody names the cook. Now the teaching. Yesterday Yudhishthira held back; tonight Bhima acts. Hindus prize ahimsa, not harming, but the Mahabharata never makes that mean standing by while someone is hurt. A warrior's dharma is protection. The poet Kalidasa explains the warrior's very name, kshatra, as the one who saves others from harm. Bhima is disguised as a cook, but his dharma isn't. Today most of us aren't warriors. Still, a protector's dharma asks something of anyone: when someone is being hurt and you can stop it or bring help, you step in, after you've listened.

811.hook: Prince Uttara boasts he'd beat the Kuru army if only he had a charioteer, and the dance teacher volunteers

811.howItsDone: Retellings of the Virata book linger on Uttara's boast and flight and on Brihannala chasing him across the field, a scene that mixes comedy with the moment Arjuna is revealed.

segments.voice: Cattle raiders. The Kauravas have heard that Kichaka is dead, and they come for King Virata's herds. The king has already ridden out to fight raiders on another side, taking Kanka, the cook and the herdsmen with him. At home, among the women of the palace, sits his young son, Prince Uttara. And Uttara talks big. If I only had a charioteer, he says, I'd beat the whole Kuru army. They'd look at me and wonder if I was Arjuna himself. The person he's talking about is standing a few feet away, in bangles.
screen: `THE KAURAVAS RAID THE HERDS.` → `UTTARA'S BOAST.` → `ARJUNA IS IN THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Sairandhri speaks up: Brihannala once drove a chariot for Arjuna. Uttara is embarrassed, but he has no one else. The teacher fumbles the armor on purpose, and the palace women laugh. Then the chariot rolls out, and Uttara sees the army: banners, elephants, Bhishma, Drona, Karna. His boast falls apart. He jumps down and runs. Brihannala runs after him, braid flying, and some Kuru soldiers think: that runs like Arjuna. The teacher catches the prince, not to shame him but to steady him. Don't be afraid, he says, in effect. You drive. I'll fight. At the shami tree Uttara unwraps the bundle and finds the great bow Gandiva. Whose are these? And Brihannala tells him: I am Arjuna. Now hold that picture, because the epic will turn it around. Soon, on the field of Kurukshetra, Arjuna himself will lose his nerve and let his bow slip, and his charioteer, Krishna, will steady him. That conversation is the Bhagavad Gita. Many readers notice the echo: the man who says you drive, I'll fight, will soon need someone at the reins for him. It's why Hindus love Krishna as Parthasarathy, Arjuna's charioteer, and temples in his name still draw crowds. The teaching: in Hindu devotion, God doesn't only watch from far above the battle. God takes the reins beside the frightened. Today fear still makes us jump from the chariot. The epic's answer isn't shame. It's someone who runs after you.

segments.voice: A conch sounds across the field, and the Kuru warriors know that sound. Arjuna is back. He fights the whole raiding army with Uttara at the reins, and in the end uses a weapon that makes the Kuru warriors fall into a stupor. He sends Uttara among them to take their fine upper cloths, for the princesses' dolls, as promised. The cattle go home. So does a prince who ran away that morning. On this last day of the Virata story, the masks come off.
screen: `A CONCH THE KURUS KNOW.` → `CLOTHS FOR THE DOLLS.` → `THE LAST DAY OF THE MASKS.`

segments.voice: Back at the palace, King Virata is overjoyed. My son has beaten the Kurus! He sits down to dice with Kanka and keeps praising Uttara. Kanka says quietly: with Brihannala driving, how could he lose? Virata, angry, throws the dice in Kanka's face. Blood runs from Yudhishthira's nose, and Sairandhri catches the drops in a vessel before they reach the floor. Brihannala is kept outside, because Arjuna has sworn that whoever draws his brother's blood outside battle will not live. The year began with dice, and it ends with dice, and the hidden king bleeding, still silent. Then the brothers walk in wearing royal clothes, take the royal seats, and Arjuna tells Virata who they are. The king offers his daughter, Princess Uttara, to Arjuna. And Arjuna says no. I was her teacher, he says, and she trusted me as a daughter trusts a father. Let her marry my son, Abhimanyu. Here's the teaching. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher sends students out into life with these words: let your mother be a god to you, your father, your teacher, your guest. Acharya devo bhava: treat the teacher as divine. It's why Hindu students touch a teacher's feet, and why Guru Purnima is a day to honor teachers. Many teachers read Arjuna's answer as the other side of it: a teacher guards that trust. Today, think of the coaches, tutors and mentors who've held yours. In Hindu teaching, that bond is sacred.
